To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the sensitization of cutaneously evoked pain after peripheral inflammation is caused by the sensitization of the primary afferent nociceptors.
peripheral inflammation causes mechanical sensitization and heat sensitization in cutaneous nociceptive afferents.

peripheral inflammation of the skin of the rat causes sensitization of nociceptors to mechanical stimulation, which can be demonstrated by the increased responsiveness of the nociceptors when they are exposed to suprathresold mechanical stimuli.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural mechanisms of nociception and pain, with particular reference to the role of the peripheral nervous system.
the mechanisms underlying the development of chronic pain.
the neural basis of pain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the sensitization of cutaneo- and articular nociceptors to mechanical and/or heat stimuli is the most likely neural mechanism of hyperalgesic and allodynic states.
the peripheral mechanisms of hyper- and allodynia are not well defined, but the central mechanisms of these sensory phenomena are well established.

peripheral inflammation causes mechanical hyperalgesic responses of nociceptors and, to a much lesser extent, heat hyperalgesic nociceptor responses, and that these are accompanied by central sensitization.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
peripheral inflammation can cause mechanical sensitization of nociceptors that is similar to heat sensitization, and that both contribute to hyperalgesia.
peripheral sensitization can account for mechanical hyperalgeisa and that central sensitization can explain heat hyperalgeisa.

The main takeaway from our work is that
mechanical sensitization of primary afferents is not an all-or-none phenomenon but can be observed as a graded phenomenon, with the magnitude of the sensitization depending on the stimulus intensity.

mechanical and thermal sensitization of cutaneously innervated nociceptors occurs after peripheral inflammation and that these phenomena are likely to be the neural bases of mechanical and thermal hyperalgesia.
